Currently we have many uses of
self.assertEqual(ans.shape, expected.shape)
self.assertTrue(np.allclose(ans.cpu(), expected, rtol=1e-02, atol=1e-03, equal_nan=True))

in our tests. e.g. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/test/test_torch.py#L11270
torch.allclose won't work well here as it only accept two tensors.
But this way is hard for backends like XLA to override precisions :P
We want to propose make an API
self.assertAllClose(torch_tensor, np_array, rtol, atol, equal_nan)

to replace it.
@mruberry @gchanan @ezyang Does this sound good?

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
For a research project, I want to implement a mixed second derivative wrt. to the input and parameters, i.e. $\partial_x\partial_\theta L(x, \theta)$. This works reasonably well using the torch.autograd.grad functionality as proven in the snippet below, but incurs significant memory overhead due to having to store a separate set of activations (which I am not sure why yet) and prohibits the use of torch.utils.checkpoint functionality if the mixed derivative happens in the checkpointing graph. Also see #24005.
On the other hand I can use the torch.autograd.backward functionality to compute the derivative, leading to significantly smaller memory requirements and compatibility with torch.utils.checkpoint, but it turns out that the parameter gradients in this case are extremely wrong.
A small script highlighting the issue is attached below.
To Reproduce
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.utils.checkpoint as cp

seed = 142


class Square(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super(Square, self).__init__()
        self.a = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1))

    def forward(self, x):
        return (self.a * x)**2


def grad_of_torch_func_backward(z, func):
    with torch.enable_grad():
        z.requires_grad_(True)
        omega = func(z).reshape(z.size(0), 1).sum()
        torch.autograd.backward(omega)
        dz = z.grad
        dz.requires_grad_(True)
        return dz


def grad_of_torch_func(z, func):
    with torch.enable_grad():
        z.requires_grad_(True)
        omega = func(z).reshape(z.size(0), 1)
        go = torch.ones_like(omega).to(z.device)
        dz = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=omega,
                                 inputs=z,
                                 grad_outputs=go,
                                 create_graph=True,
                                 retain_graph=True)[0]
        return dz


def objective_wrong_grad(model: nn.Module, y: torch.Tensor):
    y.requires_grad_(True)
    g = grad_of_torch_func_backward(y, model)
    y.requires_grad_(False)
    return y - g


def objective_correct_grad(model: nn.Module, y: torch.Tensor):
    y.requires_grad_(True)
    g = grad_of_torch_func(y, model)
    y.requires_grad_(False)
    return y - g


def correct_param_autograd():
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    se = Square()

    x = torch.ones(10, 1)
    y = x + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(x)
    z = objective_correct_grad(se, y)

    loss = cp.checkpoint(F.mse_loss, z, x)
    loss.backward()

    param_grad_correct = se.a.grad.item()
    param = se.a.item()

    return x.data.numpy(), y.data.numpy(), z.data.numpy(), loss.item(), param, param_grad_correct


def incorrect_param_autograd():
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    se = Square()

    x = torch.ones(10, 1)
    y = x + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(x)
    z = objective_wrong_grad(se, y)

    loss = F.mse_loss(z, x)
    loss.backward()

    param_grad_incorrect = se.a.grad.item()
    param = se.a.item()

    return x.data.numpy(), y.data.numpy(), z.data.numpy(), loss.item(), param, param_grad_incorrect


def compute_analytic_param_grad(a, x, y):
    return (8 * a * y * (x + (2 * a**2 - 1) * y)).mean().item()


def main():
    x0, y0, z0, loss0, p0, p_grad0 = correct_param_autograd()
    x1, y1, z1, loss1, p1, p_grad1 = incorrect_param_autograd()

    np.testing.assert_almost_equal(p0, p1)
    np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(x0, x1)
    np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(y0, y1)
    np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(z0, z1)
    np.testing.assert_almost_equal(loss0, loss1)

    analytic_grad = compute_analytic_param_grad(p0, x0, y0)
    np.testing.assert_almost_equal(p_grad0, analytic_grad)

    np.testing.assert_almost_equal(p_grad0, p_grad1)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
Expected behavior
Enable the ability to compute correct gradient wrt to the inputs using grad in conjunction with checkpointing in order to be able to scale to larger models. Alternatively enable correct mixed derivatives with backward such that the memory overhead is reduced and checkpointing can be used.

Right now the, the layout of torch/csrc/jit/ is pretty random. It's mostly flat, with some folders that may or may not make sense.
I propose reorganizing the JIT source tree to better reflect the actual components of the JIT. There are three goals for this reorg:

Help newcomers navigate the JIT codebase by providing hints about the structure. Experienced JIT developers probably know what file they need and can fuzzy search for it, thus the physical layout of the code is largely irrelevant to them.
Provide a high-level structure to help guide design. If your frontend/foo.cpp is depending on runtime/bar.h, this is a signal to reviewers that there may be unnecessary coupling.
Not be so complicated that it introduces friction. It should be super obvious from a quick ls which folder your file should go in.

The proposed layout:

frontend/: lexer/parser/ir emitter,…
runtime/: graph executor, interpreter,…
serialization/: import/export, python_print
passes/: passes
api/: Any user-facing C++/Python construct: Module, Method, Function, etc.
python/: Python bindings and python-only code
codegen/: fuser/, tensor_expr/, etc.
testing/: testing utilities
mobile/: mobile specific code (lite interpreter, etc.)
ir/: core IR abstractions and utils (ir.h, ir_views.h, etc.)

Here is a complete mapping of files to their new locations.

📚 Documentation

torch/nn/utils/rnn.html:
pad_packed_sequence doc has a confusing stand-alone statement in the description of the function:

Batch elements will be ordered decreasingly by their length.

Ordered when and where?
On the contrary the padded output is "unsorted" to how it was originally sorted when pack_padded_sequence or pack_sequence were called. So the statement in question is only correct if the original sequence was ordered decreasingly by the length of its elements and isn't necessarily the case with enforce_sorted=False.
Perhaps it should say instead:

Batch elements will be re-ordered as they were ordered originally when the batch was passed to pack_padded_sequence or pack_sequence.

But then it's possible that  sequence.unsorted_indices is None, in which case no sorting will happen.
And perhaps the sorting note would be better serving in the Returns part of the description?
Example:
seq = torch.tensor([[1,2,3,0], [4,5,0,0], [6,3,5,1]])
lens = [3, 2, 4]
packed = pack_padded_sequence(seq, lens, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)
packed
seq_unpacked, lens_unpacked = pad_packed_sequence(packed, batch_first=True)
seq_unpacked
lens_unpacked

tensor([[1, 2, 3, 0],
        [4, 5, 0, 0],
        [6, 3, 5, 1]])
tensor([3, 2, 4])
